messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Noy's Story

Noy Saengchaiyaphum was twenty-three when she was taken. She had been working late at her firm's downtown office, finishing a client reconciliation that was due the next morning. It was a Tuesday in March, unremarkable in every way until the moment the elevator doors opened on the empty thirty-second floor and a man she had never seen before stepped out. He was holding a gun. What followed was seventy-two hours in a storage unit in an industrial park—hours she has never fully articulated to anyone, hours that now, five years later, still shape every moment of her waking life.

The man had demanded money, had kept her bound, had violated her in ways that made her body feel like it no longer belonged to her. When she was finally found—when a security guard making his rounds heard her muffled cries—the police arrested him within weeks. He was convicted. He served his sentence. And then, two years ago, he was released. That fact alone had fractured something in Noy that therapy had not yet repaired. She had come to believe that the system itself had failed her, that the man responsible had paid almost nothing for what he had taken from her. The injustice of his early release felt like a second trauma layered over the first, a confirmation that what happened to her did not matter enough to the world.

But even before his release, Noy had been living a life constrained by the terror that had been installed in her body on that Tuesday. She had returned to work after three months, determined to reclaim her life, but the office felt like a trap. The open floor plan that had once seemed modern and collaborative now felt like exposure. She found herself unable to sit at her desk without positioning her chair so her back was against the wall of her cubicle, angled so she could see the entrance to her section. Her colleagues had noticed. Her manager had gently asked if everything was okay. Noy had said yes, it was fine, just a preference. But it was not a preference. It was a necessity. Without that wall behind her, she felt the phantom sensation of hands reaching for her, of the gun's barrel pressing against her spine.

At home, the hypervigilance was worse. Noy lived alone in a one-bedroom apartment in Arlington, and she had become consumed by the sounds of the building. Every footstep in the hallway, every creak of the pipes, every car door slamming in the lot below—she catalogued them all, her nervous system scanning for the one sound that would mean he had found her, that it was happening again. She had installed three deadbolts on her door. She slept with her phone in her hand. She had memorized the floor plan of her apartment so thoroughly that she could navigate it in complete darkness. When someone knocked unexpectedly—a delivery driver, a neighbor—her body would flood with adrenaline before her mind caught up to the reality of the moment. The startle was violent, involuntary. A few months ago, her upstairs neighbor had dropped something heavy, and the sound had sent Noy scrambling under her kitchen table, her heart racing so fast she thought she might be dying.

She had stopped going out in the evenings. She had stopped going to the grocery store alone. She had stopped wearing the clothes she loved because they felt like they belonged to a different person, a Noy who had not been broken. When she looked in the mirror, she felt a deep, corrosive shame that had nothing to do with her appearance and everything to do with the fact of what her body had endured. She was certain that the assault had been, in some fundamental way, her fault—that she should not have stayed late, should have been more aware, should have done something differently. The man had a gun, but in her darkest moments, she wondered if she had somehow invited this, if there was something about the way she moved through the world that had marked her as vulnerable.

At twenty-eight, Noy had been promoted to senior consultant, but the promotion felt hollow. She had missed important client dinners because the thought of being in a restaurant, unable to see all the exits, made her chest tight. Her professional relationships had atrophied. She was competent, reliable, but increasingly isolated. It was her supervisor's gentle insistence that she seek help—a comment that Noy was "not herself anymore"—that finally pushed her to call a therapist. What she wanted most was to feel safe again. What she feared most was that she never would.
